newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy calls international conference on Albania.
newsitem.headline: Italy calls international conference on Albania.

text.p: Italy on Wednesday called an international conference on Albania next month, to be attended by more than 30 delegations including the United States, as its Balkan neighbour appeared on the brink of another crisis.

The Foreign Ministry said in a statement that the conference, likely to be at foreign minister level, was planned for June 18 in Rome and would be preceded by a preparatory meeting in the Italian capital on May 26.

A ministry spokesman said senior officials from Albania, all 15 European Union countries, the United States and members of the Italian-led security force in Albania were expected to attend the planning session in two weeks' time.

They would be joined by representatives from the European Commission, the United Nations, the Western European Union military alliance, the Council of Europe, the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund and other financial institutions.
International efforts to safeguard a return to stability in Albania after its slide towards anarchy in March have so far been spearheaded by Europe.
Italy is leading a U.N.-backed force with a three-month mandate to oversee the secure delivery of humanitarian aid. It is the first such security mission to be entirely European.

Belgium and Slovenia have recently said they plan to join the force, which now comprises more than 6,000 men from Italy, France, Spain, Greece, Denmark, Turkey, Austria and Romania. Italy said on Wednesday that Portugal had also decided to join.
The statement, following a meeting of senior officials from the countries in the security force, came as tension rose in Albania over elections planned for June 29.
International mediator Franz Vranitzky prepared to race back to Tirana on Thursday for his second mission in a week after most political parties threatened to boycott the polls.

Early elections have been planned since March when Albanian President Sali Berisha agreed to share power and installed a unity government at the height of unrest which swept the country after the failure of dubious savings schemes.
The threatened boycott would make a mockery of the election just a year after the Socialist Party pulled out of the last vote in May 1996, which international observers said was flawed.
The Italian statement called on all Albanian political forces to "abstain from any initiative that could complicate the situation and to cooperate closely with the special envoy".

The latest crisis blew up after Berisha's rightist Democratic Party, which has an overwhelming parliamentary majority, pushed through an election law which the eight other parties in the unity government said was biased in Berisha's favour.

The election law was a key element of a six-point contract, signed by all nine government parties, which Vranitzky, an envoy of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, brokered during a mission to Tirana last week.
The Democratic Party has insisted its law is in line with the Vranitzky deal and agreements with other parties.
